title: IRS credit card payment fee: Split the Fee From the Tax in Your Books After T.D. 10060
excerpt: Final regulations published October 19, 2026 let the IRS collect an IRS credit card payment fee directly instead of only through a third-party processor. The fee is never a tax and never refundable, so book it on its own line. Here is the worked example, the entity-by-entity treatment, and the controls.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Worked example of an IRS credit card payment fee recorded separately from the tax, with a card statement line, an owner draw for the tax, and a fee entry
content:
The IRS credit card payment fee is not part of your tax, and after Treasury Decision 10060 it may be charged by the IRS itself. Record the fee and the tax as two separate lines, classify each by who owes it, and match the single card charge to both before you close the month.

Why this matters now

On 2026-10-19 the Federal Register published Treasury Decision 10060, Regulations Regarding Payment of Tax by Commercially Acceptable Means. The final regulations are effective the same day and apply to payments of tax and reimbursement fees made on or after that date. They carry out section 2303 of the Taxpayer First Act, which lifted the old bar on the IRS paying card processing fees as long as every dollar of fee is recovered from the people who pay by card. The regulation says the reimbursement fee "is not a tax imposed by the Code, and no portion of the reimbursement fee is eligible for refund or credit under section 6402 of the Code."

The Journal of Accountancy reported on 2026-10-16 that the rules clear the way for taxpayers to pay the IRS directly by card without being handed to a third-party processor, with the reimbursement fee collected at the time of payment. KPMG's TaxNewsFlash of the same date notes that the final rules adopt the July 2024 proposed regulations without modification. Meanwhile the IRS page on paying taxes by debit or credit card, last updated 2026-10-14, still lists two processors, Pay1040 and ACI Payments, with debit fees of $2.15 and $2.10 and credit fees of 1.75 percent and 1.85 percent, and states that no part of those fees goes to the IRS.

Trade coverage explains the rule. It does not tell a business owner what to do with the charge that lands on the card statement. That charge bundles two different things: a tax that belongs to a specific taxpayer and period, and a fee that is nobody's tax and will never come back. The fourth-quarter estimated payment is due January 15, 2027, year-end books are being closed over the next few months, and a card is the payment method most likely to be used in a hurry. Getting the split right now is cheaper than unpicking it at tax time.

What the final rule changes, and what stays the same

Three things change. First, the IRS may now sign a contract under which it pays the card processing fee itself, which the old version of section 301.6311-2 prohibited. Second, when it does, it must collect the full amount back as a reimbursement fee from card payers, paid at the time of and in addition to the tax. Third, that reimbursement fee sits outside the tax system. It is not a tax, it is not refundable or creditable, and a dispute about it goes through the card account's error resolution process under the Truth in Lending Act or the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, not through a refund claim.

Two things do not change. The IRS may still contract with processors under the familiar model, where the processor charges you directly and the IRS pays and receives nothing. As of the IRS page dated 2026-10-14 that is still the only model in operation, and neither the regulation nor the coverage gives a start date for direct card acceptance. And the rule on when a card payment counts as made is unchanged. Under section 301.6311-2(b) a card payment is deemed made when the card issuer properly authorizes the transaction, provided the payment is actually received by the United States and not returned. The authorization date on your confirmation is the payment date. The posting date on the statement is not.

For bookkeeping, the practical conclusion is the same under either model. The tax and the fee are two transactions that happen to share one card charge. Whether the fee goes to Pay1040 or to the IRS as a reimbursement fee changes the payee, not the accounting. The one thing the new rule removes is any temptation to treat a fee charged by the IRS as if it were tax. It is not, and a refund of overpaid tax will not include it.

How to record a card tax payment: two worked examples

A sole proprietor's estimated tax

Maria runs a design studio as a sole proprietor and pays her $4,000 federal estimated tax with the business credit card through a processor charging 1.75 percent. The fee is $70 and the card shows one charge of $4,070. Federal income tax on a sole proprietor's profit is the owner's personal obligation, not a business expense, and the IRS Tax Guide for Small Business says federal income tax is not deductible on Schedule C. The fee attached to a personal tax payment is personal too.

The entry on the authorization date is a debit to owner draws of $4,000 for the tax, a second debit to owner draws of $70 with a memo identifying it as the card fee, and a credit to the credit card liability of $4,070. When the card bill is paid from business checking, debit the credit card liability $4,070 and credit cash $4,070. Equity falls by $4,070, cash falls by $4,070, and profit for the month is unchanged.

Keeping the $70 on its own line matters even though it lands in the same equity account. If a bank rule later categorizes the whole $4,070 to a taxes and licenses expense, the error is easy to see when the register shows a $4,000 draw and a $70 draw next to a single $4,070 charge. It also means that when Maria's tax adviser asks how much estimated tax she paid, the answer is $4,000, not $4,070. The fee is not a payment of tax and will not appear on her IRS account as one.

An LLC's employment tax balance due

Now take a single-member LLC with two employees that owes a $1,200 balance on its quarterly Form 941 and pays it by debit card for a flat fee of $2.15. This tax belongs to the business, not the owner, so the entry is different. Debit the payroll tax liability $1,200 to clear the amount accrued when payroll ran, debit bank and merchant fees $2.15, and credit the credit card liability or cash $1,202.15. The IRS page states that card processing fees are tax deductible for businesses, and this is the kind of fee it means.

Notice what each debit does. The $1,200 reduces a liability that already existed on the balance sheet. It is not an expense in the month of payment, because the expense was recognized when the wages were earned. The $2.15 is a new expense of the month. Posting the whole $1,202.15 to payroll tax expense would double count $1,200 that was already expensed and would bury the fee. Posting it all to the liability would leave a $2.15 credit balance that never clears.

One limit from the same IRS page: federal tax deposits cannot be paid by card. Routine employment tax deposits still go through the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System. Card payments are for balances due and the other payment types the IRS lists, and each type carries a frequency limit on how many card payments it accepts in a period. If the payment register you keep for IRS payments has a column for method, this is where a card entry gets flagged for both the fee and the limit.

Accounting controls for card tax payments

Source data: the payment confirmation showing the tax amount, the fee, the authorization date, the taxpayer, the tax form, and the period; the card statement line; the bank withdrawal that later pays the card; and, for a business tax, the return or notice that created the liability. Save the IRS card payment page as it read on the day you paid, because the processors, fees, and payment types on it change, and keep the Federal Register citation for Treasury Decision 10060 with the file. Record the date each item was captured.

Calculation: tax plus fee must equal the card charge, to the cent, for every card payment. For a percentage fee, recompute it from the tax amount and the published rate and compare it to the confirmation. A difference means either the rate changed or the charge includes something else. Then total the tax lines by taxpayer and period and total the fee lines by account. The sum of the tax lines, not the sum of the card charges, is the figure that should agree with the IRS account transcript when you check it. Cash and credit card balances are point-in-time amounts. Payments and fees are flows for the period. Adding a month's card payments to a closing cash balance produces a number that means nothing.

Review: a second person, or the owner on a later day, checks that each card charge has exactly two ledger lines; that the tax line went to the account that owes it, meaning owner draws for personal income tax, a liability account for a business tax that was accrued, and an expense account only when the business tax was never accrued; that the fee line went to owner draws or to a fee expense by the same ownership test; and that the authorization date, not the posting date, is the transaction date. Any card charge from a processor or the IRS with only one ledger line is an exception.

Decision: the owner decides whether to pay by card at all, after seeing the fee next to the free alternatives, and approves each payment. The bookkeeper decides the account for each line using the ownership test and escalates anything the test does not settle. The tax adviser decides the deductibility of a fee when the entity type or the tax makes it unclear, and decides whether a returned or disputed card payment needs a replacement payment and a penalty review. Each open item gets a named owner and a date.

Limits and common mistakes

The direct IRS card option is a legal authority, not a live service. The regulation lets the IRS contract to accept cards directly. It does not say when, for which forms, or at what fee. Until the IRS payment page lists a direct option, card payments still go through Pay1040 or ACI Payments and the fee still belongs to the processor. Don't describe a processor fee as an IRS reimbursement fee in your records, because the two have different payees and different dispute routes.

Chargebacks. If a card payment is returned, the regulation treats it as never made, and the original due date still applies. Reversing the two ledger lines is the easy part. The hard part is checking whether a late payment penalty now attaches to the tax, and whether the fee was returned with it or kept. Keep the dispute paperwork from the card issuer with the payment register.

Deductibility is not a bookkeeping choice. The IRS statement that card fees are deductible for businesses covers fees on business taxes. For an individual's own income tax, the fee is a personal cost. Congress permanently ended miscellaneous itemized deductions for individuals, which is where such fees were once claimed, so a sole proprietor who books the fee on a personal estimated payment as a business expense is deducting a personal cost. Ask the tax adviser before the return is prepared, not after.

Rewards. A card that earns 2 percent back does not cancel the fee in the books. The fee is an expense or a draw on the authorization date, and the reward is recorded when it is received under whatever policy you apply to card rewards. Netting them at the time of payment hides the real cost of the method, which is the number the owner needs in order to decide whether to use a card next quarter.

State taxes. Everything above is federal. State card payment programs set their own fees, processors, and refund rules. The ownership test for the tax line still applies, but check the fee treatment separately for each state.

This article covers bookkeeping and controls. It does not say whether you should pay by card, whether a particular fee is deductible in your situation, or how to resolve a penalty. Those are questions for your tax adviser, and the posting responsibility you assign for tax payments should name who takes them there.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the IRS credit card payment fee refundable if I overpay my tax?

No. Under Treasury Decision 10060 the reimbursement fee is not a tax and no part of it is eligible for refund or credit under section 6402. A tax overpayment comes back without the fee, so your books should never carry the fee as a receivable or as part of the tax paid.

Can I deduct the fee for paying my taxes by card?

The IRS states that card processing fees are tax deductible for businesses. A fee paid on an individual's personal income tax is a personal cost, and miscellaneous itemized deductions are no longer available to individuals, so confirm the treatment with your tax adviser before classifying it.

What date is a card tax payment made?

The regulations treat a card payment as made when the card issuer properly authorizes the transaction, provided the payment is actually received by the United States and is not returned. Record that authorization date from the confirmation, not the date the charge posts to your card statement.

How should a sole proprietor record estimated tax paid by business credit card?

Debit owner draws for the tax and debit owner draws again for the fee on a separate line, then credit the credit card liability for the total charge. The estimated tax is the owner's personal obligation, so neither line is a business expense, and business profit does not change.

Does the new rule mean I can pay payroll tax deposits by card?

No. The IRS page on card payments says federal tax deposits cannot be paid by card, so employment tax deposits still go through the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System. Card payments apply to balances due and other listed payment types, subject to frequency limits.

Once each card charge is split into its tax and its fee, the monthly profit and loss statement stops carrying tax payments that were never expenses, and the figures in this monthly P and L check mean what they say.
